definition.text: The time value of money is the idea that receiving a sum of money now is generally better than receiving the same sum later.

facts.text: Money held today can be invested to earn a return, so a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future.
It is one reason interest exists: interest compensates a depositor or lender for losing the use of their money.
It compares cash flows at different dates by converting them all to one valuation date, often called time 0.
An amount PV invested at rate i grows to PV(1 + i)^n after n periods; discounting reverses this to find present value.
The present value formula is the core formula, and the others, such as the annuity formula, are built from it.
It is weighed when judging the opportunity cost of spending rather than saving or investing.
Compound interest was used in business from the Middle Ages, and pricing annuities was a key setting for developing present-value methods.
Cost–benefit analysis adjusts all costs and benefits for the time value of money, expressing them as a net present value.

title: Future value

definition.text: Future value is what an amount invested today will be worth after a given number of periods of earning interest.

facts.text: An amount PV invested at time 0 at rate i per period is worth PV(1 + i)^n after n periods.
The factor (1 + i)^n is the accumulation factor, and (1 + i)^−n is the matching discount factor.
Present value is usually below future value because money has interest-earning potential.

title: Growing perpetuity
article: Time value of money#Present value of a growing perpetuity

definition.text: A growing perpetuity is an endless stream of payments that rises at a fixed rate, valued by a simple formula when growth is below the interest rate.

facts.text: This formula is the well-known Gordon growth model used to value shares.
Few real securities grow at a fixed rate forever, but the approach is still used to value real estate, equities and other assets.

definition.text: Uncertainty describes situations where information is imperfect or unknown.

facts.text: It applies to predictions of future events, to measurements already made and to the unknown, and matters especially for decision-making.
It arises in partly observable, random, complex or changing environments, and from ignorance.
It is a state of limited knowledge in which the possible future states, their probabilities or their values cannot all be fully described.
Uncertainty can be measured only when treated as risk, by assigning probabilities to each possible outcome.
Adaptive management is an iterative way of deciding under uncertainty that aims to reduce it over time through monitoring.

definition.text: Risk is uncertainty that has been quantified: the possible outcomes have known probabilities and some of them involve losses.

facts.text: Not knowing whether it will rain tomorrow is uncertainty; giving it a probability, say from a weather forecast, quantifies the risk.
If a business event loses $100,000 when it rains and rain has a 10% chance, the risk is a 10% chance of losing $100,000.
The expected opportunity loss multiplies the chance of loss by its size, here $10,000, which suits only a risk-neutral decision-maker.
Most people would pay a premium to avoid the loss, so insurers charge more than the expected loss.
Risk differs from variability: risk concerns one uncertain future value, variability the spread of many observed values.

title: Knightian uncertainty

definition.text: Knightian uncertainty is uncertainty that cannot be measured or turned into probabilities, as distinct from measurable risk.

facts.text: Frank Knight drew the distinction in 1921, in Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit.
To Knight, risk can in principle be insured, but true uncertainty cannot.
Known risks can be insured because they have a defined probability distribution; uncertainties lack one and can lead to extreme outcomes.
Knight called those who bear uncertainty entrepreneurs, so entrepreneurship research studies how uncertainty creates opportunities.

definition.text: Radical uncertainty is uncertainty that no available means of gaining knowledge could resolve.

facts.text: John Kay and Mervyn King popularised the term in a book published in March 2020.
It differs from Knightian uncertainty in whether the uncertainty can be resolved: if research could remove it, it is not radical.

definition.text: Scientific uncertainty is often understood differently by the public than by scientists, and can be misread as ignorance or lack of consensus.

facts.text: Differences between studies caused by method can look to the public like a lack of consensus where one actually exists.
Climate change deniers followed Frank Luntz's advice to frame global warming as a matter of scientific uncertainty.
Scientific uncertainty may be managed deliberately to reach certain goals.
